meta: Nicolaes Berchem's etching Cow Drinking, made from a 1679 drawing, with far more going on than the title says.
about: The cow in this etching is not actually drinking, and the Art Institute of Chicago points out that much else is going on around it. Nicolaes Berchem was best known as a Dutch painter of calm Italian views. He also made over 50 etchings of shepherds and their animals. The museum calls this one a mature and ambitious print. Berchem based it on a drawing from 1679, which is now in Paris.

meta: The Virgin and Child appear on an altar and hand Saint Dominic a rosary in Giovanni Battista Tiepolo's altarpiece of 1730 to 1735.
about: Tiepolo shows the Virgin and Child as if they had suddenly appeared on an altar, in a vision full of light and golden clouds. The infant hands Saint Dominic a rosary. Dominic founded a preaching order that was closely tied to praying with the rosary. The embroidered scenes on the altar cloth show the mysteries of the rosary, key events in the lives of Mary and Jesus. The Art Institute of Chicago says a believer would have meditated on them while saying the prayers.

meta: Albrecht Dürer's pen drawing Young Bull, one of his earliest animal studies, made around 1496 and kept at the Art Institute of Chicago.
about: A young steer grazes in a field we cannot see. Albrecht Dürer drew it in pen and black ink, and it is one of his earliest animal drawings. The Art Institute of Chicago thinks it was probably a study from nature. Faint lines around the hind foot, back, muzzle and horns show that he first drew the animal in a slightly different pose, with its mouth open. He later reused the steer's hindquarters in an engraving of the Prodigal Son among the swine.

meta: A Day of the Dead broadside by José Guadalupe Posada, about 1910, showing skeletons that celebrate the power of the Mexican Revolution.
about: Skeletons take over this Day of the Dead broadside by José Guadalupe Posada. The Art Institute of Chicago reads the sheet as a celebration of the gleeful, destructive power of the Mexican Revolution, told through calaveras, the satirical skeletons Posada made popular. Posada illustrated thousands of cheap handbills in late 19th and early 20th century Mexico, aimed at working and middle class city readers. Later printmakers in the Taller de Gráfica Popular claimed him as their forebear.

meta: Odilon Redon's 1896 lithograph I saw above the vaporous contour of a human form, from his series after a ghost novel.
about: Redon made this lithograph for a series inspired by The Haunted and the Haunters, an 1859 novel by the British writer Edward Bulwer-Lytton. The Cleveland Museum of Art says his prints catch the mysterious tone of the book through vague imagery that sometimes borders on abstraction. Redon worked with the master printer Auguste Clot. To get the tones, he turned his lithographic crayon on its side, layered marks and even scratched into the stone.
credit_line: Gift of The Print Club of Cleveland

meta: A man and a woman ride a winged, clawed horse with a bird's head in Francisco de Goya's print Flying Folly, from a series of eighteen.
about: Seen from behind, a man and a woman ride a winged horse with claws and the head of a bird. Francisco de Goya made the print in 1815, and the Rijksmuseum says it belongs to a series of eighteen. The title is Flying Folly. The couple turn their backs to us, so we cannot read their faces.

meta: Isono Bunsai's 1829 print of Mimi de Villeneuve, the European woman who came to Nagasaki but was never allowed ashore on Deshima.
about: In 1829 a European woman, Mimi de Villeneuve, arrived in Nagasaki with her husband. European women were not allowed on Deshima, the Dutch trading post, so she had to sail back on the same ship. She never went ashore, yet pictures of her were still made. The Rijksmuseum says the text with this print describes her looks and stresses features that struck Japanese viewers as remarkable, namely her deep-set eyes, her transparent skin and her long nose.

meta: Twelve street sellers on one sheet, including a seller of matches and a seller of mussels, in Gerrit Benjamin van Goor's 1806 print.
about: Twelve street vendors share this sheet, among them a seller of sulphur matches, a mussel seller and a woman selling chestnuts. Each has a caption underneath. Gerrit Benjamin van Goor made the print in 1806, and it carries the number 3 at the top right. The Rijksmuseum holds it. The caption on this print gives a warning about taking a seller's praise of his goods at face value.

meta: Justus Rommelkop, a small man dressed as a farmer holding a glass of beer, from Pieter van Buysen's caricature series Het Dwergentooneel.
about: A small man, Justus Rommelkop, stands dressed as a farmer with a glass of beer in his hand. Verses under the picture are given in German, French and Dutch. Pieter van Buysen made the print, and the Rijksmuseum says it comes from the second Dutch bound edition of 1720. That series of caricatures of small people, known as Het Dwergentooneel, is linked to the Windhandel, the stock market frenzy of that year.

meta: Venus arrives on the shore on a shell in Sandro Botticelli's Birth of Venus, probably painted in the mid-1480s and now in the Uffizi.
about: Venus arrives at the shore, just born from the sea and already fully grown. Sandro Botticelli probably painted her in the mid-1480s, and the picture hangs in the Uffizi in Florence. It is usually discussed with his Primavera, which is also there. Art historians agree on the wedding setting and the wish to rival ancient painters, but not on who ordered the pair. They also agree that the Birth itself needs little decoding.

meta: Benjamin Robert Haydon's 1841 history painting of the World Anti-Slavery Convention at the Freemasons' Tavern in London.
about: This history painting by the British artist Benjamin Robert Haydon shows the World Anti-Slavery Convention, an abolitionist meeting held at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. The convention took place in 1840, and Haydon finished the painting a year later, in 1841. It hangs in the National Portrait Gallery in London.

meta: Two fishermen with a rod and a net stand among rocks above a pale cove in Winslow Homer's Lobster Cove, Manchester, Massachusetts.
about: Rocks fill the foreground of a cove under a pale blue sky, and pinkish cream clouds are reflected in the water. Two small fishermen in caps and blue coats stand among the rocks. One holds a rod. The other holds a net. Winslow Homer painted Lobster Cove, Manchester, Massachusetts, around 1860, and the painting belongs to the Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum in New York.

meta: Merchant Jeremiah Williams in a stern pose with papers and books, painted by Christian Gullager around 1780 for the Smithsonian American Art Museum.
about: Jeremiah Williams was a merchant from Roxbury, Massachusetts, who sold West Indian goods. In 1787 he married Matilda Davis, whose father was an important man in Boston. The museum suggests the match raised Williams's own standing. Christian Gullager painted him in handsome clothes with a stern face. Papers in his hand and books on the table behind him were a common way to show a sitter's education in colonial portraits. In the museum's reading, the picture shows the rank that men of his class hoped to reach.

meta: Johannes Kannewet's 1725 sheet of 36 winter scenes, from skating to sledging, each with a two line verse underneath.
about: One sheet holds 36 small scenes of winter pastimes, such as skating and riding sledges. Under each picture is a verse of two lines. Johannes Kannewet made the print in 1725, and the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam keeps it. The number 45 is written at the top right of the sheet, in the museum's record.

meta: Cornelis de Wael's 1602 drawing of a raid on peasants, who are tied up, killed and robbed, in the Rijksmuseum.
about: Raiders fall on a group of peasants. In the scene the farmers are tied up, killed and robbed. Cornelis de Wael made the drawing in 1602, and it is now in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. That is all the museum's short description says, and it names the attack and what happens to the victims.

meta: Charles Aubry's 1836 gazelle hunt print, one of twelve prints in a wrapper that explain different hunting methods in words and pictures.
about: A gazelle hunt fills the middle of this print. Around the main scene, different hunting techniques are explained in words and in pictures. Charles Aubry made it in 1836, and the Rijksmuseum says it is part of a wrapper that holds twelve prints. The museum in Amsterdam keeps it in its print collection.

meta: The river Waal, the city of Nijmegen and its fortifications seen from the west, in Jan Ruyter's 1738 print.
about: The river Waal runs in front of the city of Nijmegen, with the town's fortifications behind it. The view looks at the city from the west. Jan Ruyter made the print in 1738. The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam now has it in its collection, and its record describes the sheet as a view of the river, the town and its defences.

meta: A fruit tree and two hens in a fenced field in Richard Roland Holst's 1893 print Orchard in Eemnes.
about: A fenced field holds a single fruit tree and two hens pecking about. Richard Nicolaüs Roland Holst made the print in 1893, and its title places the orchard in Eemnes, a village in the Netherlands. The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam holds it. Its record lists nothing else in the field but the tree, the fence and the two birds.

meta: Edwin Lord Weeks's Hindu Merchants, painted by an artist who toured India in 1883 with a camera as well as a brush.
about: Edwin Lord Weeks traveled to India in 1883, after many years of travel through North Africa. He was a photographer as well as a painter. According to the Smithsonian American Art Museum, he wrote in his letters that he wandered the streets by day and developed his photographs at night. The museum dates this painting, Hindu Merchants, to 1880.

meta: The French artist Henry Gerbault sits behind a box of prints in Edgar Chahine's 1904 portrait, with a display cabinet and vases behind him.
about: The French artist Henry Gerbault sits on a chair behind a box of prints. Behind him stand a display cabinet and a wall hung with vases. Edgar Chahine made this portrait print in 1904. The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam owns it, and the museum's own record names the sitter as Gerbault.
